questions.title: Foundation: One component
questions.prompt: A component passes inspection with probability $0.92$. Let $X=1$ if it passes and $X=0$ if it fails. State the distribution of $X$, write its PMF, and find its mean and variance.

questions.title: Developing: Same experiment, different variable
questions.prompt: A basketball player scores each free throw independently with probability $0.7$. Classify each variable: (i) the number scored in 12 attempts, (ii) the attempt number of the first score, and (iii) the attempt number of the fourth score.

steps.title: Question (i)
steps.body: The 12 attempts are fixed and successes are counted: binomial.

steps.title: Question (ii)
steps.body: One success is fixed and trials are counted: geometric.

steps.title: Question (iii)
steps.body: Four successes are fixed and trials are counted: negative binomial.

steps.title: See the single rule
steps.body: The physical experiment is unchanged. Only the definition of the random variable changes.

questions.title: Exam: Use indicator variables
questions.prompt: A system contains 6 independent sensors. Sensor $i$ activates with probability $p_i$. Define $I_i=1$ if sensor $i$ activates and $0$ otherwise, and let $T=\sum_{i=1}^{6} I_i$. Without assuming the probabilities are equal, express $E[T]$.

steps.title: Write the count as a sum
Use linearity
steps.body: $E[T]=\sum_{i=1}^{6}E[I_i]$. Independence is not required for linearity of expectation.

questions.title: Foundation: Exactly three correct
questions.prompt: A student guesses independently on a 5-question true-or-false quiz. Let $X$ be the number of correct answers. Find the probability that the student answers exactly 3 questions correctly.

steps.title: Verify the model
steps.body: There are $n=5$ fixed independent trials and $p=0.5$ on each trial, so $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(5,0.5)$.

questions.title: Developing: At least six successful logins
questions.prompt: A login attempt succeeds independently with probability $0.7$. Eight attempts are made. Find the expected number of successes and the probability that at least 6 attempts succeed.

questions.title: Exam: Infer the parameter and solve a tail
questions.prompt: For a binomial variable $X$, the number of trials is $n=20$ and the expected number of successes is $E[X]=5$. Determine $p$. Then calculate $P(X=0)$ and $P(X\ge 1)$, explaining why the second calculation should use a complement.

steps.title: At least one
steps.body: Adding $P(X=1)+\cdots+P(X=20)$ is unnecessary. Its complement is $X=0$.

questions.title: Foundation: First success on trial three
questions.prompt: A machine starts correctly on each attempt with probability $0.4$, independently of previous attempts. Let $X$ be the attempt number of the first correct start. Find $P(X=3)$.

steps.title: Describe the required sequence
steps.body: The first two attempts must fail and the third must succeed: $F,F,S$.

steps.title: Attach probabilities
steps.body: A failure has probability $0.6$, and the success has probability $0.4$.

questions.title: Developing: Success within four attempts
questions.prompt: A data packet is delivered successfully on each attempt with probability $0.25$, independently. Find the probability that the first successful delivery occurs within the first four attempts. Also find the expected number of attempts.

steps.title: Interpret the complement
steps.body: $X>4$ means the first four attempts all fail, with probability $(0.75)^4$.

questions.title: Exam: Use memorylessness correctly
questions.prompt: A component passes a diagnostic on each independent attempt with probability $0.2$. After 5 unsuccessful attempts, what is the probability that more than 3 additional attempts are needed before the first pass? Explain why the first five failures do not appear in the final calculation.

steps.title: Name the property
steps.body: The geometric distribution is memoryless. Once the first five failures are known, the future wait behaves like a fresh geometric experiment.

steps.title: Interpret
steps.body: The known failures change neither the success probability nor the distribution of the remaining wait.

questions.title: Foundation: Third success on trial five
questions.prompt: A player wins each independent round with probability $0.5$. Let $X$ be the round on which the player records the third win. Find $P(X=5)$.

steps.title: Lock the last trial
steps.body: Round 5 must be the third win.

steps.title: Arrange earlier wins
steps.body: Exactly 2 wins must occur among rounds 1–4, giving $\binom42$ arrangements.

steps.title: Attach probabilities
steps.body: Across all five rounds there are 3 wins and 2 losses: $(0.5)^3(0.5)^2$.

questions.title: Developing: Mean and variance of the wait
questions.prompt: A recruiter hires each independently interviewed candidate with probability $0.2$. Interviews continue until 5 candidates have been hired. Let $X$ be the total number of interviews. Find $E[X]$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, and the standard deviation.

questions.title: Exam: Distinguish the mirror-image models
questions.prompt: A basketball player scores independently with probability $0.6$. Compare the following events: A = “exactly 4 scores occur in the first 7 shots” and B = “the fourth score occurs on shot 7.” Name the correct distribution for each event, write both probabilities, and explain why they are not equal.

steps.title: Event A: fixed trials
steps.body: Seven shots are fixed and successes are counted, so $P(A)=\binom74(0.6)^4(0.4)^3$.

steps.title: Event B: fixed success target
steps.body: The fourth success is fixed on shot 7, so shot 7 is a success and the first six contain exactly three: $P(B)=\binom63(0.6)^4(0.4)^3$.

steps.title: Compare the coefficients
steps.body: $\binom74=35$ while $\binom63=20$. Event A allows the fourth success to occur anywhere by shot 7; event B forces it onto shot 7.

questions.title: Foundation: Exactly two arrivals
questions.prompt: A help desk receives an average of 3 independent requests per minute. Let $X$ be the number received in the next minute. Find the probability of exactly 2 requests and state the mean and variance.

steps.title: Identify the interval mean
steps.body: The stated rate already matches the one-minute window, so $\mu=3$.

steps.title: Identify the requested count
steps.body: “Exactly 2” means $k=2$ and requires one PMF term.

questions.title: Developing: Rescale from an hourly rate
questions.prompt: Messages arrive at a stable average rate of 20 per hour. Assuming a Poisson model, find the probability that exactly 8 messages arrive during a 30-minute meeting. Identify every parameter before substituting.

steps.title: Build the interval mean
steps.body: $\mu=(20\text{ per hour})(0.5\text{ hour})=10$. The number 20 is not the mean for this shorter window.

questions.title: Exam: Convert seconds and calculate a cumulative probability
questions.prompt: A sensor records an average of 5 particle detections per minute. Detections follow a Poisson process. Find the probability of at most 2 detections during an 18-second exposure. Your solution must show the unit conversion, the new mean, and every PMF term in the cumulative probability.
